extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proof techniques / discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for constructing and checking proofs about functions (one-to-one, onto, inverses, images/inverse images) and for proofs by mathematical induction. Emphasizes proof structure, methods (element-chasing, solving equations, induction), and counterexample strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding an inverse function (formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find f^{-1}(x) solve the equation f(y) = x for y, producing a formula y = ... which defines f^{-1}(x) for x in the codomain where the equation has a unique solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for f(y)=2y, solve 2y=x to get y=x/2, so f^{-1}(x)=x/2. Emphasize solving for y and verifying uniqueness; check domain/codomain restrictions so that the resulting formula maps into the correct set. You may check directly, but theorems (e.g., 5.3.4–5.3.5) can justify equality of a guessed g and f^{-1} when compositions are identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition equal to identity implies injective/surjective
rubrics_metrics.description: If there exists g:B→A with g∘f = i_A then f is one-to-one. If there exists g:B→A with f∘g = i_B then f is onto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof pattern: assume f(a1)=f(a2), apply g to get g(f(a1))=g(f(a2)); since g∘f = i_A this yields a1=a2. Note the existential nature: assume a particular g exists. For the second part see exercises; use similar element-wise reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of bijectivity and existence of inverse
rubrics_metrics.description: For f:A→B the following are equivalent: (1) f is one-to-one and onto; (2) f^{-1}:B→A exists as a function; (3) there exists g:B→A with g∘f = i_A and f∘g = i_B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by showing 1→2 (Theorem 5.3.1), 2→3 (take g=f^{-1}), and 3→1 (apply Theorem 5.3.3). Use a circle of implications 1→2→3→1. Fill in omitted details if proofs are sketchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifying a function is the inverse: check both compositions
rubrics_metrics.description: To verify a candidate g is the inverse of f you must check g∘f = i_A and f∘g = i_B; both equalities are required to conclude g = f^{-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is possible for one composition to be the identity while the other is not; both must be checked. Examples: squaring and square-root functions show f∘g = i_B can hold while g∘f ≠ i_A if f is not one-to-one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image and inverse-image definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: For f:A→B and X⊆A define f(X) = {f(x) | x∈X}. For Y⊆B define f^{-1}(Y) = {a∈A | f(a)∈Y}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: f^{-1}(Y) (inverse image of a set) is always defined even when f^{-1} is not a function; the definition refers only to applying f to elements of A. Distinguish carefully between inverse image of a set and image under an inverse function when f is bijective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving set equality by mutual inclusion (element-chasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove two sets S=T, take arbitrary element of S and show it lies in T, then take arbitrary element of T and show it lies in S; often phrased as proving S⊆T and T⊆S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to show f(W∩X)=f(W)∩f(X) show y∈f(W∩X) ⇒ y∈f(W)∩f(X) (straightforward). The converse may require extra hypotheses (e.g., f one-to-one). Use element-chasing and the definitions of image/inverse image.

rubrics_metrics.name: When converses fail: construct counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: If a purported universal equality or implication seems false, produce a counterexample (explicit function and sets) that violates it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy used: choose a function that is not one-to-one and choose sets W and X that contain distinct elements w,x with f(w)=f(x). Example: f = {(1,4),(2,5),(3,5)} with W={2}, X={3} gives f(W∩X)=∅ but f(W)∩f(X)={5}, disproving equality. Use the attempted proof to identify where uniqueness or injectivity was needed and exploit that.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check uniqueness of solutions when defining inverse as function
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining f^{-1}(x) as the unique y with f(y)=x, ensure uniqueness; if multiple y solve f(y)=x then f^{-1} is not a function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: f(x)=x^2 from R→[0,∞) yields two solutions ±√x for x>0, so f^{-1} is not a function unless domain is restricted. Always verify the 'unique solution' condition when producing an inverse formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of proof by mathematical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ∀n∈N P(n): (1) Prove base case P(0) (or appropriate starting value). (2) Prove induction step ∀n∈N (P(n)→P(n+1)). Present final proof with explicit base case and induction step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical form: Base case: [Proof of P(0)]. Induction step: assume P(n) for arbitrary n and deduce P(n+1). Use the inductive hypothesis algebraically to derive the next case as in examples (sums of powers of 2, divisibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate base case and induction variant
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the base case that matches the domain of interest (e.g., start at n=5 when proving ∀n≥5). Variations on induction (weak vs. strong) and starting index are legitimate as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to prove 2^n > n^2 for all n≥5, take base n=5. Be explicit about why the chosen base suffices and ensure induction hypothesis covers the correct range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using existential witnesses in inductive/divisibility proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When an inductive hypothesis asserts an existential (e.g., ∃k∈Z such that 3k = n^3 − n), instantiate a witness (let k be that integer) and construct the next witness j in terms of k to prove the next case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to prove 3 | (n^3−n), assume 3k=n^3−n and compute (n+1)^3−(n+1)=3(k+n^2+n), so let j=k+n^2+n. Explicitly exhibit the constructed integer and conclude divisibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove equivalences by cycles of implications
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove several statements are equivalent, it suffices to prove a cycle of implications (e.g., 1→2→3→1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in proving equivalence of bijectivity conditions (Theorem 5.3.4). Note commentary that such proofs may be sketchy in text; students should fill in omitted details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer use of prior results to shorten proofs but fill omitted steps
rubrics_metrics.description: It is acceptable to apply previously proven theorems/exercises to obtain quick proofs, but one must be able to expand omitted steps into full arguments when required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Theorem 5.3.5 uses earlier theorems to reach g=f^{-1} quickly; a more direct but longer proof is available (exercise 10). Students should be comfortable producing full direct proofs as well as terse ones using prior results.
